extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary history / literary criticism (esp. French poetry and drama)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative principles for French poetry and tragedy from a historical-lectural perspective, explaining aesthetic defects, national tendencies, formal requirements (chorus, lyricism, unities), and practical constraints on subject choice and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a national epic before cultivating artificial species
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivation of the more artificial species was not preceded by any truly classical, successful, and national epic poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a genuinely classical/national epic as groundwork, subsequent cultivated poetic forms tend to be defective. Example: the lack of a successful French epic is cited as a chief defect of French poetry; Ronsard's attempts were insufficient. Suggested corrective: a French epic based on national history (e.g., achievements of St. Lewis) would have legitimized and strengthened later poetic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false bombast and pedantic/artificial expression
rubrics_metrics.description: When one attempts a sudden escape from barbarous rudeness, he is very apt to fall into the opposite defect of far-sought, pedantic, and artificial expression; e.g., Ronsard's style is full of false bombast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic development should not substitute one extreme for another; aim for energetic but natural expression rather than pedantry or inflated bombast. Ronsard is given as a cautionary example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of epic subject — prefer national history over absurd legends
rubrics_metrics.description: It was certainly an unfortunate idea to think of making such a foolish legend the very basis of the epopee (referring to tracing the Franks from the heroes of Troy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects rooted in authentic national history or suitably grand native traditions. Avoid building an epic upon implausible or obviously fanciful genealogical myths; use heroic national figures (e.g., St. Lewis) as more fitting epic groundwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: French tragedy should express national character and invent its own drama
rubrics_metrics.description: French tragedy ... is, without doubt, in the highest degree expressive of the peculiar turn and feeling of the French spirit and character. It is the duty of every nation to be the inventors and creators of their own drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic form should grow out of national temperament and conditions; imitation of foreign theatres is less valuable than national invention. Value lies in works that authentically reflect national feeling and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek models and the law of the three unities can be confining and absurd
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of the law of the three unities, more particularly of those of time and place, is absurd, and in total opposition to the true nature of poetry, in which we judge according to the effect produced on the imagination by a verisimilitude not historical but poetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic unity by poetical verisimilitude and imaginative effect rather than strict physical/historical possibility. The slavish application of Aristotle-as-understood by some (and propagated historically by figures like Boileau) may injure poetic freedom; Lessing's debates are relevant background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the lyrical element (chorus) in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The lyrical songs form the essential part in the tragedy of the ancients; the dialogue is a mere appendix and interlude to the chorus, not the chorus to the dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To approach the power of ancient tragedy, a dramatist needs to be at least as much a lyrical as a dramatic poet. Examples: Corneille's Cid is described as intensely lyrical; Racine restored a chorus in Athalie. When aiming for antique dignity, prioritize lyric/choral elements alongside dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of the chorus leads to interpolated intrigues or rhetoric of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the lyrical part is taken away, the plot was found to be too little to fill up the tragedy, and recourse was had to... a crowd of interpolated intrigues ... or else the whole was filled up with that rhetoric of the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of padding a thin plot with unnecessary subplots or excessive rhetorical speeches; both are harmful to the dignity and purpose of tragedy. The omission of lyrical material often produces these compensatory faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric of passions strengthens national expression but can be overdone
rubrics_metrics.description: This rhetoric of the passions has lent to it a strength which it wants in all other respects ... Besides, a certain measure of this rhetoric is a necessary and indispensable element of all dramatic representation. The thing is... overdone in the French tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical, passionate speeches can effectively express national character and give strength, but should be balanced—excess weakens dramatic structure. Accept some rhetoric as indispensable, but avoid its predominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of oratory over dramatic unity in French tragedy (audience judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the audience is founded much more upon the oratory of the individual speeches, than the dramatic connection and effect of the whole piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and practitioners should be aware of this national tendency and strive to balance memorable oratory with coherent dramatic architecture; do not rely solely on fine speeches to carry a play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination/denouement: tendency toward complete destruction (tragic ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in this respect, the French tragedy is the child of the antique; that its termination is in general one of complete destruction, or that, if there be any softening, the sorrow still continues to be by far the predominant material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For traditionally antique/tragic effect, endings of overwhelming loss or destruction are common and appropriate; notable exceptions (considered positive) are works where Christian victory or blessedness emerges (e.g., Racine's Athalie, Voltaire's Alzire). Use such deviations consciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/composition timing — inspiration can trump tedious elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Another great rule ... is the one borrowed from Horace, according to which a work of intellect should be as many years before it is published, as a human child lies months in the womb before it is born. ... the Athalie of Racine, and the Cid of Corneille ... were neither of them subjected to any such process of tedious elaboration, but both brought at once before the world in the inspiration and glow of their first conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that long, tedious elaboration is always superior; some great works are produced in their first inspiring conception and succeed without protracted maturation. Evaluate on result and vitality, not solely on time spent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish adherence to mechanical precepts (Boileau's rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Boileau's well known maxim, 'of a rhyming couplet the last verse should, if possible, be first made.' ... instead of the true judgment and feeling of art, in his own criticism, he is fond of a species of ridicule ... and, instead of poetry, he is most anxious for a full and perfect rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical trickery (forcing rhyme, formulaic rules) should not replace genuine poetic judgment and feeling. Criticism and poetic practice should privilege art and feeling over mechanical precepts exemplified by Boileau.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints lead to foreign subjects in French tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of its earlier productions are almost never taken from their own national history. The circumstance is probably to be explained by the want of any successful and universally known French epic poem. Besides, the most tragical incidents in the old French history could not fail to excite disagreeable recollections and comparisons, ill adapted for the purposes of a stage entirely dependent upon the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that political/cultural realities (lack of celebrated national epic, court censorship/sensitivity) have shaped subject choices toward foreign material. When possible and safe, choosing national subjects can strengthen national feeling on stage; otherwise, be aware of these practical limitations.
